query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (around 1–2 atomic percent) of molybdenum to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will form a dispersion of fine Mo-rich precipitates that improve its strength–ductility balance, creep resistance, and corrosion stability under aerospace-relevant conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform fine lamellar microstructure that exhibits good strength and plasticity but limited long-term creep and corrosion resistance.
generation.intervention: Addition of 1–2 atomic percent molybdenum (Mo) to the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, sustained mechanical loading including room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments simulating aerospace fastener service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, uniformly distributed Mo-rich precipitates within the lamellar matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Mo-rich precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and stabilize the microstructure against coarsening and phase separation during thermal and mechanical stresses, thereby enhancing strength and creep resistance, while also promoting a more protective surface passivation to lower corrosion rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved balance between strength and ductility, reduced creep strain under long-term loading, and enhanced corrosion resistance compared to the baseline alloy, all without sacrificing ductility.
generation.baseline: The unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, which despite its fine lamellar structure, falls short of meeting the rigorous long-term creep and corrosion requirements of aerospace applications.
generation.boundary: The anticipated improvements are expected only with precisely controlled Mo additions (around 1–2 at%) and proper processing to maintain the uniform lamellar structure; deviations could lead to embrittlement or formation of coarse, detrimental precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in mechanical and corrosion performance under cyclic and extreme thermal conditions may vary with processing conditions and long-term environmental exposure, requiring further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one with the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition and one with an additional 1–2 at% Mo. Process both under identical conditions. Subject the samples to tensile testing, creep experiments under sustained loading, and corrosion tests in a simulated aerospace environment. Conduct microstructural characterizations to confirm the formation and uniformity of Mo-rich precipitates.
measurements: Creep strain rate and time to rupture
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloy does not exhibit significant improvements in the balance of strength and ductility, a measurable reduction in creep strain or an enhanced corrosion performance relative to the baseline alloy, or if the ductility is substantially compromised, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A minor microalloying addition of molybdenum (Mo) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its strength–ductility balance as well as its resistance to room-temperature creep and corrosion by stabilizing the lamellar microstructure through the formation of fine Mo-rich precipitates.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform fine lamellar structure that shows suboptimal mechanical performance under aerospace-relevant conditions.
drafts.intervention: Incorporate a small amount (approximately 1–2 atomic percent) of Mo into the alloy composition during processing.
drafts.conditions: The alloy will be subjected to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep tests, and corrosive environments that mimic aerospace fastener service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The Mo is expected to promote the formation of fine, stable Mo-rich precipitates and adjust the lamellar interphase spacing, thereby reinforcing the microstructural framework.
drafts.mechanism: By increasing lattice distortion and facilitating the nucleation of Mo-rich precipitates along the lamellar interfaces, the added Mo is anticipated to hinder dislocation motion and creep, while also enhancing the alloy’s passivation characteristics to reduce corrosion.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Mo-modified alloy should display a more balanced strength–ductility profile, lower creep strain under sustained loads, and improved corrosion resistance under cyclic and aggressive environmental conditions.
drafts.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, which, despite its favorable uniform lamellar structure, falls short of industrial and aerospace performance requirements.
drafts.boundary: This improvement is expected only for minor doping levels (around 1–2 at% Mo) that preserve the fundamental eutectic and lamellar structure. The extent of the improvement may depend on optimized processing conditions and thermal treatments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of samples: one with the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition (baseline), one with 1 at% Mo, and one with 2 at% Mo added. Subject each set to cyclic thermal loading, sustained mechanical creep tests at room temperature, and standardized corrosion tests in a simulated aerospace environment. Compare the performance metrics of strength, ductility, creep strain, and corrosion rate across the samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped samples (either at 1 or 2 at%) do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in the targeted properties (strength–ductility balance, reduced creep strain, and lower corrosion rate) compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a small concentration (approximately 1–2 atomic percent) of molybdenum to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will form stable precipitates that improve creep resistance and corrosion performance without compromising ductility.
drafts.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with uniform fine lamellar microstructure and baseline strength/ductility balance but limited creep and corrosion resistance.
drafts.intervention: Introduce 1–2 at.% Mo into the base alloy via conventional melting and casting, followed by standard homogenization and heat treatment for homogeneous distribution of the Mo-containing precipitates.
drafts.conditions: Processing under inert or vacuum atmosphere to ensure minimal contamination, and controlled solidification kinetics to preserve a refined lamellar microstructure during Mo addition and subsequent heat treatment.
drafts.structural_mediator: Fine, uniformly distributed Mo-rich precipitates within the previously established lamellar matrix, providing enhanced obstacle hardening and improved local chemical stability.
drafts.mechanism: The Mo-rich precipitates act as stable pinning sites that impede dislocation motion, increasing strength under elevated temperature and long-duration stress (improved creep resistance) while also contributing to enhanced passivation behavior to reduce corrosion rates.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, the Mo-containing alloy is expected to show measurably improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures (e.g., at least a 20% increase in creep rupture life) and lower corrosion rates without substantial harm to room-temperature ductility.
drafts.baseline: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy without Mo addition, known to have good strength and ductility but lacking in long-term creep and corrosion resistance.
drafts.boundary: Excessive Mo additions (>2 at.%) or inadequate control of solidification may lead to coarse or undesired phase formation, potentially degrading ductility and corrosion resistance. The proposed benefit is primarily expected under load at moderate to high temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloys: the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and one with 2 at.% Mo. Cast both under identical conditions, homogenize them, and machine test specimens. Perform standard creep tests at multiple stress levels and temperatures (e.g., 700–800 °C). Evaluate corrosion rates in a simulated aerospace/space environment. Compare measured creep strain rate, time to rupture, and corrosion current density between the two alloys.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time under constant load.
Corrosion current density and passivation characteristics under relevant environmental conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-containing alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in creep life or corrosion resistance compared with the baseline alloy (values overlap within experimental error), or if its ductility is substantially reduced, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a small addition of titanium (Ti) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its strength–ductility balance and enhance its creep resistance under extreme temperature fluctuations by promoting the formation of nanoscale precipitates that impede dislocation motion and stabilize the microstructure.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
drafts.intervention: Add 1–2 atomic percent titanium (Ti) to the alloy composition.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is subjected to extreme temperature fluctuations (e.g., -100°C to 600°C), long-term mechanical loading, and room-temperature creep tests.
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates within the lamellar structure.
drafts.mechanism: The Ti-rich precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion, enhancing strength, while their nanoscale size and distribution maintain ductility. Additionally, the precipitates stabilize the microstructure against coarsening and phase separation under thermal and mechanical stresses, improving creep resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a 15–25% increase in yield strength and a 10–20% improvement in ductility compared to the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy. Creep resistance will also improve, with a reduction in creep rate by at least 20% under identical testing conditions.
drafts.baseline: The mechanical properties and creep resistance of the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
drafts.boundary: The improvement is expected to hold for Ti additions in the range of 1–2 atomic percent and under temperature fluctuations up to 600°C. Excessive Ti addition (>2 atomic percent) may lead to embrittlement or undesirable phase formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys with 0%, 1%, and 2% Ti additions. Characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to confirm the formation of nanoscale Ti-rich precipitates. Perform mechanical testing (tensile tests) to measure yield strength and ductility. Conduct creep tests at room temperature and under cyclic temperature conditions (-100°C to 600°C) to evaluate creep resistance.
measurements: Creep rate under room-temperature and cyclic thermal conditions
Microstructural analysis of precipitate size and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if Ti addition does not lead to the formation of nanoscale precipitates, or if the modified alloy shows no significant improvement (less than 5%) in strength, ductility, or creep resistance compared to the baseline material.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled heat treatment process will enhance the strength and ductility of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
drafts.conditions: Heat treatment at specific temperatures and durations to optimize microstructure.
drafts.structural_mediator: Refinement of grain structure and phase distribution due to heat treatment.
drafts.mechanism: Heat treatment will promote recrystallization and phase transformation, leading to improved mechanical properties.
drafts.predicted_outcome: An increase in both strength and ductility compared to the untreated alloy.
drafts.baseline: Current performance of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, which does not meet industrial requirements.
drafts.boundary: Effects observed under standard atmospheric conditions and within the temperature range typical for aerospace applications.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a comparative study with two groups: one subjected to controlled heat treatment and one left untreated.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size and phase distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in strength and ductility compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introduction of a controlled amount of carbon (C) as an alloying element to form carbides can enhance the strength and stability of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure
drafts.intervention: Addition of carbon (C) to form carbides
drafts.conditions: Extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion
drafts.mechanism: Carbide precipitation can act as obstacles to dislocation movement, enhancing strength, and potentially improving resistance to creep and corrosion by reducing grain boundary diffusion and reactivity
drafts.predicted_outcome: Improved strength-ductility balance, enhanced stability under extreme conditions, and potentially improved resistance to creep and corrosion
drafts.baseline: Current performance of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy
drafts.boundary: Optimal amount of carbon addition, processing conditions to ensure uniform carbide distribution, and maintenance of the fine lamellar structure

falsification_experiment.design: Systematic variation of carbon content in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, followed by mechanical testing (tensile, creep), corrosion testing, and microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of carbon does not result in a significant improvement in strength-ductility balance or stability under extreme conditions without compromising ductility, the hypothesis is falsified
